item.title: The Opposite of Distraction Is Not Focus: It's Reverence
item.description:
Attention

The Opposite of Distraction Is Not Focus: It's Reverence

"Focus" has become industrial, and it is burning us out. It's time to seek awe.

Posted August 14, 2026

Key points
  • Focus can narrow attention without making life feel more intimate, humane, or alive.
  • Distraction may be less a failure of discipline than a cultural crisis of intimacy.
  • Reverence invites us back to depth, fulfillment, and profound curiosity.

It is often assumed that the opposite of distraction is focus. While that may be technically true, focus itself is not inherently healing or therapeutic.

You can focus on a spreadsheet, a work assignment, a resentment, or even a doom-scroll. Focus only means that attention has narrowed. It does not tell us whether attention has become more intimate.

When Focus Isn’t Enough

I understand that, in the most literal sense, distraction and focus can be discussed as narrow and wide apertures of attention, like a camera. Sometimes that “lens” is useful. But in my therapy work—especially when collaborating with individuals with mental health concerns related to ADHD, anxiety, depression, or occupational burnout—distraction often presents as a symptom of distress, not merely a deficit of attention.

Here, narrow versus wide may not be the most meaningful distinction. A person can be narrowly focused while existentially absent. There are many techniques to help someone concentrate or find enough motivation to push through the day. But if I reach for such an intervention as a clinical reflex, the client may remain unseen.

Higher functioning is not always higher functioning.

Moreover, self-improvement is not confirmation that we have addressed the environmental conditions or the real human suffering.

Clinically, I find it more relevant to explore distraction in the context of depth and fulfillment.

The Industry of Attention

Much of modern life trains us toward partial contact. Consider the ambient social pressure to psychologically compress a walk into steps, a meal into calories, a sunset into content. Our bodies become collections of metrics.

Optimization culture is rendering our flesh into machinery and the human mind, with all its capacity for wonder and authenticity, into another artificial intelligence. We even download apps to lock us out of other apps. This all suggests that our compulsion to solve problems may itself be one of our biggest problems.

If we accept that the opposite of distraction is focus, we trap ourselves in the very machine language that systemically exhausted us in the first place.

Focus is industrial.

A Crisis of Intimacy

I have come to believe the opposite of distraction is not focus. The opposite of distraction is reverence.

I know that word may sound religious. Secularly speaking, we need a word serious enough to buck the trend of making everything casual, swipeable, and, most unfortunately, disposable.

You do not “execute” reverence. You are stopped by it.

If we look at the etymology of reverence, we find a clue to wresting intimacy back from the increasingly involuntary patterns that keep us engaged yet disenchanted. The word comes from the Latin revereri and means to stand in awe or respect.

Research on awe helps illuminate this. In one series of experiments, people who experienced awe reported feeling as though they had more time available. They were also less impatient and showed a greater willingness to give their time to others.

This matters because distraction often comes with a sense of time poverty. And this makes sense given how much time gets harvested into screen time, a euphemism for a pseudo-dissociative state. The impact is that we feel rushed, fragmented, behind, or subtly hunted by the next thing.

Reverence interrupts that trance and reminds us that a tree is not just “another thing”—a material resource for paper and wood—but a unique marvel of nature.

Another study highlights how fragile intimacy can be in the presence of technology. In experiments with face-to-face conversation, the mere proximity of a mobile phone was associated with lower reported conversation quality, closeness, and connection.

Distraction is more a cultural crisis of intimacy than a failure of discipline.

Returning to Deep Contact

The prefix re- in reverence signals “back” or “again,” as in “to remember” or “to restore.”

It implies that our default, natural state is one of awe, humility, and deep contact with the world around us. Distraction is what happens when we are pulled away from that baseline. Therefore, reverence is not a new skill we must master, nor a productivity hack we must learn.

It is permission to return to profound curiosity, where the wholeness of being meets the majesty of the universe.

item.title: Why We Learn Connections That Aren't Really There
item.description:
Autism

Why We Learn Connections That Aren't Really There

What autism can teach us about how our brains decide what matters.

Posted August 14, 2026

We are constantly learning from experience, trying to figure out what predicts good outcomes and what predicts bad ones. The challenge is that the world is noisy. Every experience contains countless details, only some of which actually matter. To learn efficiently, the brain has to decide what deserves credit for an outcome — and what should simply be ignored. Remarkably, it often gets this wrong.

Imagine giving a presentation that goes particularly well. You were well prepared, your argument was clear, and the audience was engaged. But the experience contained many other details too: the room you were in, where you stood, what you ate that morning, even the shirt you happened to be wearing. Most of these things had nothing to do with your success. Yet our brains are remarkably good at learning these associations, even ones that aren't really there.

This may be one reason people develop lucky rituals, become superstitious, or form strong intuitions based on coincidences. A shirt worn during a successful presentation becomes a "lucky shirt." A particular routine performed before a win starts to feel essential. Somehow, information that happened to accompany an outcome becomes part of what we think produced it. In psychology, this problem is sometimes called credit assignment: when something happens, what deserves the credit—or blame?

Source: ds stories/ Pexels

But our tendency to incorporate information that shouldn't matter extends beyond learning causal relationships. Consider a choice between two medical procedures. One has a 90% survival rate. The other has a 10% mortality rate. These are, of course, exactly the same odds. Yet most of us don't experience them as the same. The way the information is presented can change how we feel about it and, sometimes, what we choose. This isn't exactly the same as mistakenly learning that your lucky shirt caused a good presentation. But the two phenomena share something important: information that should not determine our judgment nevertheless finds its way in.

Psychologists have documented many such examples. Our decisions can be influenced by money we've already spent and cannot recover, by irrelevant alternatives, and by our intuitions about what "feels" right. These tendencies are so common that psychologists have long considered them part of our predictably "irrational" nature. If these tendencies are such a fundamental feature of human cognition, an interesting question follows: Are they inevitable?

A different pattern in autism

Over the past decades, research on autism has offered an intriguing answer.

Autism is usually studied in terms of the difficulties associated with it, particularly in social communication and behavior. Yet autistic individuals can also show intact or even enhanced abilities in some domains. Several years ago, my colleagues and I reviewed a particularly striking example. Across different studies, autistic individuals appeared less susceptible to several of the biases that commonly influence non-autistic people. Their choices were less affected by framing, sunk costs, irrelevant alternatives, and some forms of intuitive reasoning.

article continues after advertisement

We called this pattern enhanced rationality: in certain contexts, autistic individuals appear to make more rational judgments and decisions, seemingly less influenced by information that should not objectively affect them. Of course, autism is highly heterogeneous, and these group-level patterns do not describe every autistic individual. But what might explain this pattern?

One possibility is that autistic and non-autistic people differ in how they select and weigh information. Our brains rarely approach a new situation from scratch. We use context, previous experience, emotions, and expectations to interpret what is happening now. These shortcuts are enormously useful. Without them, navigating the complexity of everyday life would be almost impossible. But they can also introduce information that leads us away from what is actually relevant.

This made us wonder whether the differences observed in autism might begin earlier. Most studies of enhanced rationality had examined the decisions people ultimately made. But what if the difference begins while people are still learning what matters?

What do we actually learn from experience?

In a recent study of adults who reported a clinical autism diagnosis, my colleagues and I tested exactly that. Participants repeatedly chose between different shapes, each associated with a changing probability of receiving a monetary reward. To do well, they had to keep learning which shapes were currently more rewarding.

But each shape also happened to appear either on the left or the right side of the screen. That detail was completely irrelevant. Locations were randomly assigned and had no relationship whatsoever to reward. We explicitly told participants this and even tested that they understood it. And yet, non-autistic participants learned from location anyway.

After receiving a reward, they became slightly more likely to choose the same location again, even when entirely different shapes appeared there. Nothing about the objective environment had made that location more valuable. Yet after it happened to be paired with a reward, participants began behaving as though it had. The brain had learned an association that wasn't actually present in the environment, and that association then influenced the next decision.

article continues after advertisement

Autistic participants showed substantially less of this tendency. They were better at assigning credit to what actually predicted the reward while largely ignoring a feature that did not. And the pattern wasn't limited to the two diagnostic groups: across the entire sample, people reporting more autistic traits also tended to show less learning from irrelevant information. In this particular environment, autistic participants' learning therefore more closely reflected the actual structure of the task.

The reality we learn

It's not that one way of processing information is universally better. There may be very good reasons that our brains learn broadly. Outside the laboratory, nobody tells us which information is relevant. The detail that seems meaningless today might turn out to predict something important tomorrow. Our previous experiences and expectations help us navigate that uncertainty quickly and efficiently.

But sometimes, they also lead us to learn relationships that were never actually there. And this is where autism may offer a particularly interesting window into how all of us construct our understanding of the world. Two people can encounter exactly the same information yet learn something different from it. Once that happens, their next decisions are no longer guided by quite the same representation of reality.

This is part of what fascinates me about the gap between objective and subjective reality. We often think of beliefs as ideas that we consciously hold about the world. But some of the assumptions that guide our behavior may begin much earlier, in the basic process of learning from experience: what we notice, what we ignore, and what our brains decide was responsible for what happened.

The world provides us with experiences, our brains decide what those experiences mean, and what we learn becomes part of the reality that guides whatever we do next.

item.title: The Art of Anticipation
item.description:
Happiness

The Art of Anticipation

The surprising power of giving yourself something to look forward to.

Posted August 14, 2026

Key points
  • Your brain is future-oriented and constantly anticipating what comes next.
  • Looking forward to different experiences can create positive emotion before they happen.
  • You can intentionally plan things to look forward to instead of waiting for them to happen.
Source: Lia bekyan / Unsplash

“What are you looking forward to?”

It seems like a simple question. Yet when I ask people, many pause much longer than they expect. Some eventually smile and mention an upcoming vacation or a family celebration. But just as often, the answer is, “I don’t know” or “I haven’t thought about it.”

Those answers say something important. Many people spend so much time managing today’s responsibilities that they don’t intentionally create things to look forward to.

But one of the most powerful ways to improve our emotional well-being is to deliberately create positive experiences to anticipate.

It’s what your brain was built to do.

Your brain is fundamentally future-oriented. Every moment it is asking, What happens next? It is constantly making predictions about the future and using that information to decide where to direct your attention, energy, and behavior. Rather than simply reacting to the world around you, your brain is continuously preparing for the world it expects is coming.

This remarkable ability is one of the reasons humans have been so successful. It allowed our ancestors to prepare for changing seasons, search for food before they became hungry, and avoid danger before it arrived. That same system is responsible for many of your emotions.

When you think of a future you don’t want, you experience stress, anxiety, and other negative emotions.

However, when you think of a desired future, you experience positive emotions.

That is because the brain’s reward system, which releases feel-good neurotransmitters such as dopamine, becomes active when we expect something positive to lie ahead. Looking forward to an experience generates motivation, directs attention, and creates positive emotion long before the event itself occurs.

Think about how you feel before leaving for a long-awaited vacation. The vacation may last a week, but the excitement often begins months earlier. Planning the trip, imagining the places you’ll visit, and counting down the days all become part of the reward.

The same thing happens on a much smaller scale. Trying a new restaurant. Buying tickets to a concert. Planning a weekend hike. Signing up for a class you’ve always wanted to take. Meeting an old friend for lunch. Exploring a neighborhood you’ve never visited. None of these experiences need to be extraordinary. Their emotional power comes from the anticipation they create.

article continues after advertisement

Unfortunately, many people gradually stop feeding this system. Life becomes organized almost entirely around responsibilities. Work deadlines replace personal adventures. Calendars fill with meetings, appointments, errands, and obligations. We become remarkably efficient at managing our lives while unintentionally removing many of the experiences that generate excitement about the future.

The result is more than boredom. Without realizing it, we deprive ourselves of one of the brain’s most reliable sources of positive emotion. This may be one reason people sometimes describe feeling emotionally flat, even when nothing is particularly wrong. They are managing the present well, but they have stopped actively creating a future that feels exciting.

Anticipation, however, is not something you have to wait for. It is something you can create.

This is where agency becomes so important. Most people think of anticipation as something life gives them. They wait for someone to invite them somewhere, for a holiday to arrive, or for an opportunity to appear. But your emotional life changes the moment you reverse that relationship.

Instead of asking, “What do I have coming up?” ask, “What can I give myself to look forward to?”

It doesn’t have to be expensive or dramatic. Schedule one new experience every month. Take a different route home and explore a part of your city you’ve never seen. Plan a day trip. Register for a cooking class. Start learning a language before a future trip. Invite friends to a dinner you’ve been meaning to host. Buy tickets to a lecture, a play, or a concert several months away.

None of these suggestions are about escaping your life. They are about enriching it. Every time you intentionally create something to anticipate, you are doing more than making plans. You are giving your brain evidence that good things are ahead. That expectation changes how you experience today.

Perhaps the most important question isn’t whether you are happy right now. It’s whether your future contains enough reasons to feel hopeful, curious, excited, and engaged.

article continues after advertisement

The future is one of your greatest psychological resources. The art of anticipation is learning to use it intentionally.

So, what are you looking forward to?

If the answer isn’t immediate, perhaps today is the perfect day to give yourself something worth anticipating.

item.title: Neurodiverse Sexuality and Common Challenges
item.description:
Sex

Neurodiverse Sexuality and Common Challenges

People with ADHD and/or on the autism spectrum encounter similar sexual issues.

Posted August 14, 2026

Key points
  • Many more people are being diagnosed with ADHD and autism than in past generations.
  • Neurodiverse folks often share similar sexual challenges, like impulsivity or sensory stimulation challenges.
  • Using communication and planning, neurodiverse people and their partners can enjoy a delightful sex life.

An increasing number of people are being diagnosed with Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD) and Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD), sometimes both at the same time (AuDHD). This has become so common that people who are trying to destigmatize such neurodiversity have crafted new words to describe the population of folks with varied thought and processing differences. Rather than disabled or disordered, some people prefer to refer to others and themselves as neurospicy.

Image: Colorful handprints with words
Source: Polina Kovaleva/Pexels

This rise in diagnosis does not necessarily mean that more people have autism or ADHD today than in years past. Instead, lack of awareness in previous decades meant that this range of diversity went undiagnosed for many people, especially women. Increasing knowledge has led to a significant uptick in diagnosis among adults, and especially Millennials and Gen Z. Sometimes adults who bring in their children for diagnosis also find themselves matching many of the diagnostic criteria and realize later in life that they too have autism, ADHD, or sometimes both.

Neurospicy folks share some common traits when it comes to sexuality and gender, some of which I explored in a blog on BDSM and neurospicy folks. Many people with ADHD and/or autism find the intricacies of social rules and expectations to be confounding rather than obvious or commonsensical. Exposing conventional expectations as socially constructed means that many neurospicy folks feel less bound by these apparently random rules that masquerade as inevitable but are in fact made up. On the positive side, seeing through the veneer of social expectations grants neurospicy folks significant freedom to be authentic and consider their own needs and boundaries. On the challenging side, being rejected and shamed for neurospicy behaviors or ideas can push many people with autism or ADHD to mask their true responses and attempt to conceal their diversity behind a façade of neurotypical behaviors. One of the ways in which this conundrum expresses itself is via sexuality and sexual relationships.

If you are neurospicy yourself, love someone who is, or provide mental health care for folks in this category, it can be important to understand some of the social differences that shape sexual interactions and behaviors for neurospicy people.

Sex and Relationship Issues for Neurospicy People

While many people in general have alexithymia — which is difficulty identifying or communicating emotions — it is especially common among people with ADHD and autism. This can unfortunately lead to misunderstandings among partners who are hoping to connect on a deep emotional level — especially if one of them is neurospicy and another is neurotypical. Neurotypical partners can benefit significantly from understanding the neurospicy person’s perspective on the world, and it can help them to understand when the neurospicy partner does something that might seem initially nonsensical. It is likely that the neurospicy person has already been attempting to understand the neurotypical people around them, even before they engaged in a romantic relationship.

Image: head with colorful squiggles
Source: Tara Wimstead/Pexels

Even in relationships where everyone is neurotypical, communication can be challenging. Add a mismatch in neurotype and opportunities to miscommunicate abound. For example, people with ADHD can be impulsive and find tracking daily tasks or details to be difficult. Remembering to use birth control correctly (such as taking birth control pills at the same time every day) can be a challenge for neurospicy folks who end up having a higher rate of unplanned pregnancy.

ADHDers have higher levels of hypersexuality and problematic pornography use, and report more relationship issues like affairs/infidelity and divorce. Their frequent difficulty with transitions (a common issue for neurospicy folks) can include sexual transitions as well, and attention problems can translate to either/both distraction during sex and/or hyperfocus that leads to low or absent sexual desire or hypersexuality. Even though they may crave sexual novelty and intensity, neurospicy folks might also have sensory issues that make engaging in new and/or intense interactions kind of tricky for them.

Neurospicy folks frequently experience intense emotional reactions and report more sexual distress and dysfunction than neurotypical people do. These challenges also operate in neurospicy folks’ daily lives outside of sexuality and can sometimes lead to fear of intimacy and social masking to blend in with neurotypical society. Fear of intimacy can be especially daunting in romantic relationships where masking can be difficult to sustain when spending a lot of time together. Collectively, these issues can create challenges with partners who feel hurt, don’t understand, or are mystified by how to handle their partner’s sudden shifts, emotional moods, or impulsive actions.

Neurospicy Friendly Sexuality

This is not to say that all neurospicy folks and their partners are doomed to sexual disaster. In fact, neurospicy folks can make fascinating, exciting, and adventurous partners. They can be chatty, bubbly, and charismatic people who enjoy sex and make great lovers. Some neurospicy folks report that sex can help them manage their ADHD symptoms, with “post nut clarity” (the clear mind that happens for some people after orgasm) improving focus and decreasing distractibility.

One way to make sex more genial for neurospicy folks is to communicate about it beforehand. Exploring in conversation what kind of novelty each person might enjoy can open doors to exciting experimentation. Partners can also discuss various forms of sensory stimulation to find out what types feel good and what is overstimulating. Ideally, these conversations would include not only the kinds of touch that are stimulating in a pleasant way, but also the sights, smells, tastes, and other sorts of tactile interactions that can shape a sexual encounter. Finally, making a sex plan can help to alleviate anxiety for everyone involved. Talking about how to get started, what to do during sexual interactions if things start to feel off, and how to end the interaction on a positive note can set the stage for a more satisfying sexual session. Identifying things like code words to express a large cluster of connected feelings or signals to help modulate the pace of action allows people to communicate without disrupting the flow. Letting a partner know if it is important to cuddle after having sex can keep them from getting up to wander away and inadvertantly hurting their lover's feelings. With care and conversation, sexuality can be great for neurospicy folks and the people who love them!

item.title: This Common Online Habit Slowly Drains Your Happiness
item.description:
Happiness

This Common Online Habit Slowly Drains Your Happiness

A highly normalized habit can do an unexpected amount of damage.

Posted August 14, 2026

Source: fauxels / pexels

Most people assume the online habit doing the most damage to their mood is something personal: too much scrolling, too many arguments in the comments, too much bad news. But one of the most comprehensive recent looks at internet use and wellbeing — published in the 2026 World Happiness Report from Oxford’s Wellbeing Research Centre and Gallup — points somewhere less intuitive. The habit that matters most isn’t really a personal one at all. It’s the automatic way people calibrate their own online behavior to match everyone around them.

The Online Habit Has A Name: Keeping Pace

Keeping pace, or the reflex of treating “how much everyone like me is online,” acts as the invisible baseline for how much online activity is considered normal, healthy, or expected. A 2024 study published in Frontiers in Psychology also found that among adolescents, perceived peer norms track closely with how much they themselves post, react, and stay online.

Researchers behind the happiness report found something similar at the population scale: the same hour of internet use can be harmless, even beneficial, for one person and quietly corrosive for another, depending almost entirely on how saturated that person's social world already is with heavy use.

In a peer group where social media use is still relatively uncommon, more time online tends to track with slightly better well-being. But once a peer group crosses a high-saturation threshold, that same hour starts tracking with worse well-being, and the effect gets stronger the more universal heavy use becomes.

This is a meaningful addition to the common claim of “screens are bad.” It says the damage isn’t just a private transaction between a person and their phone. It’s also a social contagion of expectation. In other words, everyone is quietly adjusting to whatever level of use has become unremarkable in their world.

Why This Habit Hits Some Generations Harder Than Others

The finding helps explain something that’s puzzled researchers for a while: young people report the steepest declines in well-being tied to internet use, even though their raw usage differences from a few years ago aren’t dramatically larger. It isn’t primarily about how much more they’re using their phones — for many young adults, social media use is now close to universal in almost every country studied. It’s that they have almost no low-saturation peer group left to serve as a comparison point. There’s no version of “normal” available to them that isn’t already heavily online, so the environment offers no natural brake.

Older adults, by contrast, still live in more varied digital environments — some peers are heavy users, many aren’t — which seems to let each person’s own usage matter more on its own terms, without inheriting the runaway momentum of a fully saturated peer group.

Beating This Habit Is Not Really About Willpower

article continues after advertisement

This is where the finding gets uncomfortable for anyone hoping self-discipline alone will fix it. As a 2025 review published in Frontiers in Psychology lays out, a growing body of research finds that perceived norms — not actual ones — are what most consistently drive people’s online behavior. If the harm scales with how saturated your surrounding peer environment is, then cutting your own use in a highly saturated world only partially insulates you — you’re still living inside a social norm engineered to make heavy use invisible and moderate use feel like abstinence. Trying to opt out entirely, alone, works against the current rather than with it.

The mechanism traces further than mood. Rising internet use in saturated environments tracks with real declines in interpersonal trust — a relationship a 2025 study published in Frontiers in Sociology also found using nationally representative Chinese survey data — alongside a shrinking sense of social connectedness and, notably, a sharper drop in how people rate their own social life compared to peers, even when their actual offline socializing hadn’t changed nearly as much. The damage often shows up first in perception, before it shows up in anyone’s actual calendar.

The point isn’t that anyone needs to quit their phone, or that screen time itself is the villain. It’s that the meaningful variable is environmental, not individual — which peer groups, families or friend circles someone spends time in matters as much as anything they do alone with an app.

Seeking out relationships and communities where heavy use isn’t the unquestioned default may do more for someone’s happiness than any personal screen-time rule ever could, because it changes the baseline being measured against, not just the behavior being measured.

The habit worth breaking, in the end, isn’t checking a phone too often. It’s mistaking a saturated environment for a neutral one.

A version of this post also appears on Forbes.com.

item.title: 5 Reasons the Emotional Lives of Parents Matter
item.description:
Parenting

5 Reasons the Emotional Lives of Parents Matter

How parents relate to emotions affects themselves—and their children

Posted August 14, 2026

Key points
  • Emotions are contagious and can affect how we think and respond to our children.
  • Children learn from us how to feel about feelings.
  • Our past experiences with challenging emotions can show up in our parenting.

Every parent has feelings. Some emotions we relish, like love, joy, pride, and excitement. Other emotions make us struggle, like frustration, anger, fear, sadness, guilt, and embarrassment.

Whether we like them, hate them, or ignore them, all these feelings are a normal part of being human—and they inevitably become part of the parenting experience.

Source: Hilary Jacobs Hendel

Understanding our emotional lives can help us become more present, connected, and resilient parents.

Here are five reasons the emotional lives of parents matter for our own and our children’s well-being.

1. Emotions are contagious

Parents naturally have painful emotions like anxiety, fear, and anger. If we are not aware of them, these feelings can affect the people around us in non-verbal communications such as our tone of voice, facial expressions, and body posture. Without awareness and tools to work with our own feelings, we may be unwittingly communicating them to our child.

When children pick up on our emotions through our tone of voice and facial expressions, their nervous system responds. After all, we are wired for emotional communication starting from birth onward. So, for example, you may be angry at your boss, but your child may feel you are angry at them. They are too young to discern that Mommy is angry—and her anger is directed at her boss, not me. By knowing that emotions are contagious, parents can take greater care to check their non-verbal communication.

2. Our emotions influence how we respond to our children

Children can push our buttons in surprisingly powerful ways. A tantrum may trigger anger. A teenager pulling away may bring up fear or sadness. And even more complex, our child’s struggles may activate our own old experiences.

When we can name, validate, and work with our emotions, we are empowered with choice and greater self-control. Instead of automatically reacting, we can pause, get curious about what we’re feeling, and respond in a way that reflects our values.

3. Children learn from us about how we handle emotions

Children learn about emotions by watching us.

Our children watch us judge our emotions. They watch us avoid them. They watch us criticize others for their feelings. But they also watch us validate our emotions. They watch us show empathy for others who are experiencing emotional pain. They watch us offer support rather than judge others or ourselves as “too needy.”

When we can acknowledge our feelings without being overwhelmed by them, we teach our children that emotions are not something to fear or be ashamed of; they are a part of being human.

article continues after advertisement

For example, saying, “I’m really annoyed right now. I need a minute to calm down,” models how we can validate an emotion and take a positive step to calm ourselves. This teaches a constructive way to deal with anger instead of lashing out.

4. Our past can show up in our parenting

Sometimes our reactions to our children are bigger than the situation seems to warrant.

That’s often a clue that something deeper has been activated. A child’s neediness, anger, independence, or distress can touch emotional experiences from our own childhood. For example, if our own parent criticized us for making mistakes, when our child makes a mistake, we may impulsively do the same. Not only may this cause a backlash of guilt, but it carries forward through the generations the lesson that mistakes are bad instead of a natural part of learning.

Becoming aware of these patterns helps us distinguish between what belongs to the present and what belongs to the past. That awareness leads to more freedom in responding the way we intend, rather than reacting from old emotional wounds.

5. Parents have emotional needs, too

Parents are often encouraged to put their children’s needs first. But ignoring our own emotional needs doesn’t make us better parents.

We need support, rest, connection, and opportunities to process our own emotions. When we care for our emotional lives, we increase our capacity to be attuned and present for our children.

Taking care of ourselves isn’t selfish. It’s part of taking care of our families.

Most people still don’t know that ignoring or burying core emotions like anger and sadness creates or exacerbates anxiety and depression. Tools like the Change Triangle and techniques like grounding, breathing, and validating our sadness, fear, and anger show us the way to calming our nervous system. A regulated nervous system allows us to be an openhearted parent who prioritizes connection and compassion even as we set the rules of the household.

No parent is perfectly calm, patient, or emotionally regulated all the time. We will get overwhelmed. We will yell. We will misunderstand. We will say things we regret. What matters most is what happens next.

The emotional lives of parents matter because our inner lives inevitably shape our relationships with our children. When we become more comfortable with our own emotions, we make more room for our children to become comfortable with theirs.
